risk equalisation is a policy instrument that can be used to advance public policy objectives in VHI markets, but its implementation is complex and countries must consider carefully how it fits into their overall health policy objectives.

the three case studies show that the introduction of VHI markets is not a simple process.

The main takeaway from our work is that
risk equalisation in voluntary insurance is not a simple policy tool, but one that needs to be carefully designed to avoid the risk of perverse incentives.

countries considering introducing risk equalisation in voluntary markets need to carefully consider how to structure the subsidy to ensure that it is affordable and that risk selection is not incentivised.

the introduction of VHI markets does not change the role and importance of risk equalisation as a tool to meet the related public policy goals of risk solidarity and efficiency in health care provision.
